::: {.callout-note .se-question appearance="simple"}
## The question

[What is the ideal $(x,y)^2$?](https://math.stackexchange.com/questions/4733892/what-is-the-ideal-x-y2), asked by [yuuu](https://math.stackexchange.com/users/908119/yuuu) on Mathematics Stack Exchange (2023-07-10; [CC BY-SA 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by-sa/4.0/)):

> I am reading this [article][q-1] and in page 6 there is an exercise to show that the ideals $(x,y)$ and $(x,y)^2$ define the same blowup of the affine space $A^2$ when taken as a center. 
>
> I have two questions:
>
> What exactly is the ideal $(x,y)^2$? I would like to understand who are the elements of this ideal.
>
> Also, I would appreciate some hint about how to solve this exercise. Maybe considering that the two of them define the same zero locus?
>
> Thanks in advance.
>
>
>   [q-1]: https://homepage.univie.ac.at/herwig.hauser/Publications/ggt05-hauser.pdf
:::

The product of two ideals $I$ and $J$ is the ideal $IJ$ generated by all products $ab$, where $a \in I$ and $b \in J$.

The square of an ideal $I$ is the ideal $I^2 = II$. So it is generated by all products $ab$, where $a,b \in I$.

The ideal $(x,y)$ in the ring $K[x,y]$ is generated by $x$ and $y$. So $(x,y)^2$ is generated by $x^2$, $xy$, and $y^2$.
